title: CAN-SPAM Act
tagline: The US law that decides what a compliant cold email actually has to include.
excerpt: The US law setting the rules for commercial email: accurate sender info, honest subject lines, a working opt-out.
definition: A US federal law governing commercial email, requiring accurate sender details, a clear physical address, a working unsubscribe link, and non-deceptive subject lines.
body: Unlike some other regions, the US doesn't require prior opt-in for B2B cold email, which is what makes cold outreach legally viable there in the first place. But every message still needs an honest 'From' line and a real way to opt out, and violations carry real financial penalties per email.

schemaDescription: The CAN-SPAM Act is a US law that sets the rules for commercial email, requiring accurate sender information, a working unsubscribe mechanism, and honest subject lines, with penalties for violations.
metaDescription: What the CAN-SPAM Act requires for commercial email, who it applies to, and what B2B cold email needs to stay compliant with it.

faqs.question: What is the CAN-SPAM Act?
faqs.answer: The CAN-SPAM Act is a US federal law, passed in 2003, that sets rules for commercial email. It requires accurate sender details, non-deceptive subject lines, a valid physical postal address, a clear way to opt out, and honouring opt-out requests promptly. It covers business-to-business email as well as consumer email.

faqs.question: Does CAN-SPAM allow cold email?
faqs.answer: Yes. CAN-SPAM does not require prior consent, so cold email to US business contacts is legal as long as every message follows its rules: honest sender details and subject line, a physical postal address, a working unsubscribe option, and opt-out requests honoured within 10 business days.

faqs.question: What are the penalties for violating CAN-SPAM?
faqs.answer: Each email that violates CAN-SPAM can bring a separate civil penalty, and the US Federal Trade Commission adjusts the maximum for inflation every year, putting it above $50,000 per email. Both the company whose product is promoted and the company that actually sent the email can be held responsible.
